title: Genetic Discovery and Fine-Mapping of Multivariate Latent Factors
author: Astle, Butterworth, et al.
materials: custom code for INTERVAL NMR analyses

steps.title: Download GWAS summary data
steps.instruction: Obtain the complete set of GWAS summary statistics for the blood cell traits from the FTP sites listed in the key resources table (or from the NHGRI‑EBI GWAS Catalog). Also download the phenotypic covariance matrix and the association and linkage‑disequilibrium summary statistics for the SMIM1 region from https://github.com/jennasimit/flashfmZero-example-data.

steps.title: Index summary‑statistics files
steps.instruction: If a summary‑statistics file is not indexed, compress it with bgzip and create a tabix index using the chromosome identifier in column 3 and the 1‑based physical position in column 4. Example commands: `bgzip -c MFR_chr1.tsv > MFR_chr1.tsv.gz` and `tabix -s 3 -b 4 -e 4 MFR_chr1.tsv.gz`.

steps.title: Install and load R packages
steps.instruction: In R, install BiocManager if missing, then install all required packages listed in the protocol, install the remotes package, install flashfmZero from GitHub, and finally load flashfmZero.

substeps.instruction: for (pkg in packages) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) { BiocManager::install(pkg) } library(pkg, character.only = TRUE) }

steps.title: Remove traits with excessive missingness
steps.instruction: Read the comma‑separated file `traits.csv` (traits in columns, header row). For each trait compute the fraction of missing values and discard any trait whose missing‑data fraction exceeds 0.50 (half of the participants).

steps.title: Compute and prune trait correlation matrix
steps.instruction: Calculate the correlation matrix of the retained traits. Build an adjacency matrix where an entry is TRUE if the absolute pairwise correlation ≤ 0.99. Iteratively remove the trait with the highest degree (most connections) until no adjacency entry exceeds the 0.99 threshold, guaranteeing that no three retained traits have all pairwise correlations > 0.99. Save the names of the kept traits to `selected_phenotypes.tsv`.

substeps.instruction: while (any(adj_mat)) { deg <- rowSums(adj_mat); remove_index <- which.max(deg); adj_mat[remove_index, ] <- FALSE; adj_mat[, remove_index] <- FALSE }
write.table(as.data.frame(colnames(Y_start)[traits_to_keep]), file = "selected_phenotypes.tsv", col.names = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE, sep = "\t")

steps.title: Harmonise GWAS summary statistics
steps.instruction: Read the regional summary statistics for each phenotype, store them in a list of data frames, and run `harmoniseGWAS` with the specified arguments. The function will return columns named `beta`, `SE`, `rsID`, and `EAF`. Ensure no missing variant IDs and that the same ID is used across all GWASs.

substeps.instruction: MFR_ss <- scanTabix(MFR_ss_tabix, param = region) %>% unlist() %>% paste(collapse = "\n") %>% read_tsv(col_names = FALSE)

obsgwas <- harmoniseGWAS(obsgwas, minMAF = 0.005, minINFO = 0.4, beta_colname = "EFFECT", se_colname = "SE", snpID_colname = "ID_dbSNP", EA_colname = "ALT", NEA_colname = "REF", EAfreq_colname = "ALT_FREQ", BP_colname = "BP", pvalue_colname = "P", INFO_colname = "INFO")

steps.title: Run Bayesian fine‑mapping
steps.instruction: Apply the flashfmZero fine‑mapping functions to the harmonised GWAS data for each latent factor. Extract credible sets and variant marginal posterior probabilities (MPP). Report variants with MPP > 0.90 and SNP‑group level probabilities (MPPg).

description: In this protocol we demonstrate how to calculate latent factor genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics and how to perform single- and multi-trait Bayesian fine-mapping of latent factors using the flashfmZero R package.1,2 We begin from GWAS summary statistics computed for each phenotype in complete blood count (CBC) reports measured using Sysmex XN analysers on the European genetic ancestry study participants in the INTERVAL BioResource.3,4 CBC reports are used clinically to determine properties of the peripheral blood. They generally incorporate a standard set of (‘classical’) traits, including measurements of the concentration of hemoglobin, measurements of the concentrations of the principal types of blood cell and measurements of the average volumes of red cells and platelets. In this example, we also include so-called ‘non-classical’ CBC (ncCBC) traits that do not appear in standard CBC reports but that are measured by the Sysmex XN, such as cell-type specific measurements of average cell granularity and cell nucleic acid content. Collectively, the blood traits we consider exhibit a complicated correlation structure, partly because all types of blood cell derive from a common stem cell type —the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) —and partly because different types of mature blood cell interact, for instance, in hemostasis and in immune responses. In the protocol, we demonstrate the derivation of latent factor GWAS summary statistics for chromosome 1 and demonstrate Bayesian fine-mapping of latent factors in a region of chromosome 1 containing SMIM1, a gene that expresses small integral membrane protein 1, a transmembrane protein underlying the Vel blood group.5,6 Variants in the SMIM1 locus, including an expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) of the gene and a frameshift variant responsible for the Vel blood type, have been associated with a wide variety of phenotypes relating to red blood cell biology.3,4,7,8,9,10,11,12 The complete set of summ
